questions.prompt: Consider the statements: I: All Booklets are Manuals. II: All Manuals are Catalogues. If both are true, which conclusion can conclusively be drawn?
hints: Translate each “all” statement into a subset relation.
Chain the two inclusions; their converses need not hold.
questions.solution: Let B,M,C denote the three sets. The hypotheses give B⊆M and M⊆C, hence B⊆C. Thus every booklet is a catalogue. Reverse inclusions are unsupported: for example B={1}, M={1,2}, C={1,2,3} satisfies both hypotheses and falsifies all three other options.
questions.theory: A set is a collection of objects, and a subset relation means that every member of one collection belongs to another. The statement “all X are Y” is the inclusion X⊆Y; it does not assert Y⊆X. Inclusion is transitive: X⊆Y and Y⊆Z imply X⊆Z. Venn diagrams divide a union into disjoint membership regions, so each printed regional count is counted once in the total. An intersection of two sets may include their triple intersection; “exactly two” expressly excludes that central region. When interpreting an unlabelled diagram, compare containment and overlap relations, rather than the apparent sizes of the curves. Ordinary category meanings determine inclusion, while the drawing does not imply numerical cardinalities. A useful check is to supply an object in each visibly allowed region and see whether its proposed category memberships are consistent.

similar_questions.prompt: All roses are flowers and all flowers are plants. What follows?
similar_questions.solution: Writing R⊆F⊆P gives R⊆P, so all roses are plants. Neither converse follows; a grass plant is a counterexample to plants being roses.

similar_questions.prompt: All squares are rectangles. Must all rectangles be squares?
similar_questions.solution: No. A rectangle of side lengths 2 and 3 belongs to the rectangle set but not the square set, so the reverse inclusion fails.

questions.prompt: What is the unit digit of 1³+2³+3³+4³+5³+6³+7³+8³+9³?
hints: Use the sum-of-cubes identity.

questions.solution: The identity Σ(k³)=[n(n+1)/2]² gives (9·10/2)²=45²=2025. Its units digit is 5.
questions.theory: A base-ten two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b has numerical value 10a+b, where 1≤a≤9 and 0≤b≤9. Writing ab in a number puzzle denotes this positional value, not the product a times b. The unit digit of an integer is its remainder modulo 10. Congruences can be added and multiplied: replacing each term by a congruent integer preserves the remainder of the final expression. For powers, unit digits often repeat cyclically, and for sums one can also exploit an algebraic identity. The sum of the first n cubes is [n(n+1)/2]² for nonnegative integer n. First express the quantity algebraically, then reduce only as much as needed. Common pitfalls are dropping a place-value factor of ten and reducing an exponent without checking its actual cycle length.

questions.theory: A coding or relationship puzzle is solved by translating each assertion into a precise constraint. A substitution code assigns a fixed digit or symbol to each letter; repeated letters must therefore receive repeated symbols. A letter not present in the example remains unspecified unless an additional rule is stated. Avoid inventing an alphabetic rule from a single example or confusing the person in a photograph with that person's parent.

questions.prompt: A circle of radius 1 is cut into four quarters and rejoined into the shape shown (four circular arcs forming a curved hourglass outline). What is the shape’s area?

questions.solution: The drawing rejoins the four quarter-circle boundary arcs, alternating two convex arcs and two concave arcs. A quarter-circle arc of radius 1 has a chord of length √(1²+1²)=√2. The four joining chords form a square with area (√2)²=2. Each circular segment between an arc and its chord has area π/4−1/2. The upper and lower segments add to the square, while the left and right segments subtract. Hence total area is 2+2(π/4−1/2)−2(π/4−1/2)=2. questions.theory: A circular sector of radius r and angle θ in radians has area r²θ/2. The isosceles triangle joining its center to the two arc endpoints has area r²sinθ/2, so the circular segment between the chord and arc has area r²(θ−sinθ)/2. A quarter-circle has θ=π/2, chord length r√2, and segment area r²(π/4−1/2). Equal convex and concave segments cancel. Rearranging boundary arcs does not preserve the enclosed area in the way rearranging nonoverlapping filled pieces does; one must follow the pictured boundary. Chord lengths and sector angles determine the geometry, and all areas scale quadratically with r.

For infinite domains even a finite codomain of size at least two can yield uncountably many functions: binary-valued functions correspond to subsets, and Cantor's theorem makes the power set of ℕ uncountable. Over a finite field of q elements there are qᵐ−1 nonzero m-vectors, and each one-dimensional subspace contains q−1 nonzero vectors. The finite-field assumption matters: counting scalar representatives without dividing by q−1 overcounts each matrix.

questions.prompt: X is the real vector space of twice differentiable real functions on [0,1]. Define φ:X→ℝ³ by φ(f)=(f(1),f′(1),f″(1)). Which is true?
hints: Construct a quadratic with any prescribed value and first two derivatives at 1.

questions.solution: For any (a,b,c)∈ℝ³, f(x)=a+b(x−1)+(c/2)(x−1)² has φ(f)=(a,b,c), so φ is onto. The first isomorphism theorem gives X/ker φ≅im φ=ℝ³, hence dimension 3. The functions (x−1)ᵏ, k≥3, lie in ker φ and are linearly independent, proving the kernel and X are infinite dimensional.
questions.theory: For a linear map T:V→W, its kernel consists of vectors sent to zero and its image consists of all attained outputs. The quotient V/ker T identifies vectors whose difference lies in the kernel. The first isomorphism theorem gives V/ker T≅im T, regardless of whether V is finite dimensional; therefore a finite-dimensional image yields a finite-dimensional quotient even when the original space and kernel are infinite dimensional. Evaluation of a function and its derivatives at a fixed point is linear. Polynomials in powers of x−a provide prescribed derivative data through their Taylor coefficients, and sufficiently high powers annihilate all low-order derivative evaluations. Distinct monomials are linearly independent because a zero polynomial has every coefficient zero. Avoid applying finite-dimensional subtraction to two infinite dimensions.

similar_questions.prompt: On polynomials define T(p)=(p(0),p′(0)). Find quotient dimension.
similar_questions.solution: The polynomial a+bx attains any (a,b), so T is onto ℝ². The quotient by its kernel is isomorphic to ℝ² and has dimension 2; the kernel contains all powers xᵏ for k≥2.

similar_questions.prompt: Let T:ℝ⁴→ℝ² be T(a,b,c,d)=(a+c,b+d). Find kernel dimension.
similar_questions.solution: T is onto. Kernel vectors satisfy c=−a,d=−b, giving basis (1,0,−1,0),(0,1,0,−1) and dimension 2.

questions.theory: An eigenvalue λ of a square matrix A is a scalar for which Av=λv for some nonzero vector v. Constant row sum s makes the all-ones vector an eigenvector with eigenvalue s. questions.prompt: For n≥1 define fₙ∈C[0,π] by sin(nx)/sin x for 0<x<π, fₙ(0)=n, fₙ(π)=(−1)ⁿ⁻¹n. Let V=spanℝ{f₁,f₂,f₃}, with ⟨f,g⟩=(2/π)∫₀^π f(x)g(x)sin²x dx. Which is true?

hints: The weight sin²x cancels the denominators in the products.

questions.solution: For positive m,n, ⟨fₘ,fₙ⟩=(2/π)∫₀^π sin(mx)sin(nx)dx=δₘₙ. This follows by the product-to-sum formula, with integral π/2 when m=n and zero otherwise. Thus f₁,f₂,f₃ are orthonormal, hence independent and a basis of their span, of dimension 3. The same identity gives f₄ orthogonal to V with norm 1; if f₄ belonged to V it would be orthogonal to itself, impossible. Only B is true.
questions.theory: An inner product is a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space. A family is orthogonal if distinct vectors have zero inner product and orthonormal if each vector also has norm one. Any finite orthogonal family of nonzero vectors is linearly independent: take inner products with each member in a proposed zero combination to obtain its coefficient. Weighted integral inner products ∫fgw are positive definite on continuous functions when the nonnegative weight is positive throughout the interval interior. Isolated endpoint zeros do not affect positivity. Sine functions on [0,π] satisfy ∫sin(mx)sin(nx)=0 for distinct positive integers and π/2 for equal indices, proved through product-to-sum identities. Scaling by 2/π normalizes their norms. Boundary extensions affect continuity, but endpoints do not change the integral.

similar_questions.prompt: Normalize sin x under the ordinary L² inner product on [0,π].

similar_questions.prompt: If u,v are orthogonal and have squared norms 2 and 3, find ‖2u−v‖².

questions.prompt: V={ax³+bx²+cx:a,b,c∈ℝ}. For f∈V define Q(f)=∫₋₁¹(f′(t))²dt. Which assertion is FALSE?

options.A: Q is a positive definite quadratic form on V.

hints: Expand the square of f′+g′.

questions.solution: Q is quadratic, and Q(f)≥0. If Q(f)=0, continuity and nonnegativity imply f′≡0, hence f is constant. V contains no nonzero constants, so f=0; Q is positive definite. Also Q(x)=∫₋₁¹1dt=2. For any r>0, Q(√(r/2)x)=r. But Q(x+x)=Q(2x)=8, while Q(x)+Q(x)=4. Thus D is false; the missing cross term is 2∫f′g′.
questions.theory: A real quadratic form Q comes from a symmetric bilinear form B through Q(v)=B(v,v), and satisfies Q(cv)=c²Q(v). It is positive definite if Q(v)>0 for every nonzero v. Integral expressions such as ∫(f′)² are automatically nonnegative, but their kernel must be checked: derivative zero means a constant function, so positivity depends on whether nonzero constants are allowed in the underlying space. Continuity ensures that a nonnegative integrand with zero integral vanishes everywhere. Quadratic forms are generally not additive; expansion gives Q(u+v)=Q(u)+2B(u,v)+Q(v). Positive scaling lets a nonzero positive quadratic form attain every positive value. Confusing a quadratic form with a linear functional is the central pitfall; homogeneity has degree two, not one.

similar_questions.prompt: On V=span{x,x²}, is ∫₀¹(f′)² positive definite?

questions.prompt: Let f:ℂ→ℂ be a polynomial. For R>0 let γ_R(t)=Re^{2πit}, 0≤t≤1. Suppose ∫₀¹|(f∘γ_R)(t)γ_R′(t)|dt→c∈ℝ as R→∞. Which is FALSE?
hints: The displayed absolute value gives an integral of magnitudes, not a signed contour integral.
For a nonzero degree-d polynomial, its modulus on a large circle is uniformly comparable to Rᵈ.
questions.solution: Suppose f≠0 has degree d≥0 and leading coefficient a_d≠0. Uniformly in θ, f(Re^{iθ})/(a_dRᵈe^{idθ})→1, so for sufficiently large R, |f(Re^{iθ})|≥|a_d|Rᵈ/2. Also |γ_R′(t)|=2πR. The integral is therefore ≥π|a_d|R^{d+1}→∞, contrary to its finite limit. Hence f≡0, and c=0. This makes A,B,C true and c>0 false.
questions.theory: A polynomial's leading term controls its growth uniformly on large circles. If f(z)=a_dzᵈ plus lower-degree terms with a_d≠0, the sum of lower terms divided by |a_d|Rᵈ tends to zero uniformly for |z|=R. Thus its modulus is eventually bounded below by a positive multiple of Rᵈ. The parameterized circle γ_R(t)=Re^{2πit} has speed |γ_R′|=2πR, so integration of |f(γ_R)γ_R′| measures the magnitude of f integrated against arc length. It is fundamentally different from a complex contour integral ∫f(z)dz, where cancellations can yield zero for every polynomial. A finite limiting magnitude integral excludes every nonzero polynomial, including a nonzero constant. Always locate absolute-value bars precisely before applying Cauchy's theorem or asymptotic arguments.

similar_questions.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀¹|γ_R′(t)|dt for γ_R=Re^{2πit}.
similar_questions.solution: The speed is constant 2πR, so the integral is 2πR, the circumference; it diverges as R→∞.

similar_questions.prompt: Compare ∮_|z|=R z²dz with ∮_|z|=R |z²||dz|.
similar_questions.solution: The analytic integral is zero because z² has primitive z³/3. The magnitude integral equals R² times circumference 2πR, hence 2πR³.

questions.prompt: Let X be the image of [0,1] under f(z)=(z−i)/(z+i). Which is true?

options.A: X is the line segment joining −1 and −i.
options.C: X is the line segment joining −1 and 1.

hints: For real x, numerator and denominator have equal modulus.
Find the endpoint images and the signs of real and imaginary parts for 0<x<1.
questions.solution: For real x, f(x)=[(x−i)²]/(x²+1)=(x²−1)/(x²+1)−i·2x/(x²+1), with |f(x)|=1. It sends 0 to −1 and 1 to −i, with both real and imaginary parts negative in between. More explicitly f(x)=e^{i(π+2 arctan x)}. As x rises from 0 to 1, that angle rises continuously from π to 3π/2. Thus X is exactly the lower-left quarter of the unit circle, option B.
questions.theory: A Möbius transformation (az+b)/(cz+d), with ad−bc≠0, is a bijection of the extended complex plane and maps generalized circles to generalized circles. A generalized circle is either a circle or a line, with the point at infinity included for lines. For a real variable x, the Cayley transformation (x−i)/(x+i) has modulus one because x−i and x+i are complex conjugates. To identify an interval image, endpoint images alone are insufficient: a circle has two connecting arcs, and one must determine the interior location or a continuous argument. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate separates real and imaginary parts. A parameter such as arctan x then identifies the traversed angular interval. Avoid replacing a curved arc with the straight chord connecting its endpoints.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the image of [0,∞) under (x−i)/(x+i).
similar_questions.solution: The angle π+2arctan x ranges from π toward 2π, excluding 2π for finite x. Thus the image is the lower semicircle from −1 inclusive to 1 exclusive.

similar_questions.prompt: Compute the image of x=√3 under the same transformation.
similar_questions.solution: The angle is π+2π/3=5π/3. Thus the image is 1/2−i√3/2, also obtained from real part (3−1)/4 and imaginary part −2√3/4.

questions.prompt: Which assertion is true? There exists an entire function f such that, for every positive integer n:
hints: Taylor coefficients are derivatives divided by n!.
An entire function requires infinite radius of convergence; examine the nth roots of the coefficients.
questions.solution: For A the Taylor coefficient is a_n=1/nⁿ, so |a_n|^{1/n}=1/n→0. The series a₀+Σₙ≥₁zⁿ/nⁿ has infinite radius and defines the required entire function. For B, coefficients nⁿ have nth roots n→∞, giving radius zero. For C, coefficients 1/n have nth roots tending to 1, giving radius 1. For D, coefficients n also have nth roots tending to 1, giving radius 1. Uniqueness of Taylor coefficients rules out alternative entire functions satisfying those latter derivative data.
questions.theory: An entire function is holomorphic on all of ℂ. Its Taylor expansion at zero is f(z)=Σa_nzⁿ with coefficients a_n=f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n!, and the series converges throughout the plane. The Cauchy–Hadamard formula states 1/R=limsup|a_n|^{1/n}, with R=∞ when that limsup is zero and R=0 when it is infinite. Derivative prescriptions therefore determine all nonconstant Taylor coefficients and leave only the constant term free. A power series with infinite radius constructs the desired entire function, whereas a finite radius proves that no entire function can have those coefficients, by uniqueness of analytic expansions. The factorial division is essential: the growth of the derivatives themselves cannot be used as though they were the power-series coefficients.

similar_questions.prompt: Can an entire function satisfy f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)=1 for every n≥1?
similar_questions.solution: Coefficients are 1/n!, whose nth roots tend to zero. The function eᶻ−1, with arbitrary added constant, satisfies the requirement.

similar_questions.prompt: Can an entire function satisfy f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)=n!2ⁿ?
similar_questions.solution: Coefficients 2ⁿ have nth-root limit 2, so radius is 1/2. They produce 1/(1−2z) near zero, which has a pole; no entire function exists.

hints: A line is not an open subset of the complex plane.

questions.solution: If f were nonconstant, the open mapping theorem would make f(ℂ) open in ℂ. A subset of the line y=x+1 cannot contain a nonempty open disk, so f is constant, say f≡c on that line. Then c/z→0 as |z|→∞. The line does not contain zero, so c≠0: |f| stays finite and positive, |zf| diverges, and f does not tend to zero. Thus only B is true.
questions.theory: The open mapping theorem says that a nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected open domain sends open sets to open sets. In particular, a nonconstant entire function has an image open in ℂ. A line, circle, or other set with empty interior cannot contain such an image; holomorphic functions whose values are constrained to these sets must therefore be constant. This argument does not require boundedness, unlike Liouville's theorem. One can also derive constancy from the Cauchy–Riemann equations when real and imaginary parts satisfy a linear relation. Once constancy is established, evaluate each claimed asymptotic behavior for that constant, including whether zero belongs to the prescribed image set. A constant function need not be zero, and multiplying it by z and dividing it by z have very different limits.

similar_questions.prompt: If an entire function has real values everywhere, prove it is constant.
similar_questions.solution: The real axis has empty interior, whereas a nonconstant holomorphic image is open. Therefore the function is constant.

similar_questions.prompt: An entire function has values on |w|=3. Find the limit of f(z)/z.
similar_questions.solution: The circular image restriction forces f≡c with |c|=3. Hence |f(z)/z|=3/|z|→0.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true?

options.A: p∤1+(p−1)! for some odd prime p.
options.C: There exist a∈ℤ and a prime p>11 with p∤aᵖ−a.
options.D: p∤(p²)!/(p!)² for some odd prime p.

hints: Recall Wilson’s theorem and both forms of Fermat’s little theorem.
Factor 1234, and count the p-factors in the factorial quotient.
questions.solution: Wilson gives (p−1)!≡−1 mod p for every prime, so A is false. Since 1234=2·617, every prime p>700 is coprime to 1234; Fermat gives 1234^{p−1}≡1 mod p, proving B. Fermat also gives aᵖ≡a for all integers a, disproving C. For D use Legendre: v_p((p²)!)=p+1 and v_p((p!)²)=2. The quotient has p-adic valuation p−1>0, so p divides it for every odd prime. Thus D is false.
questions.theory: Fermat's little theorem states aᵖ≡a modulo a prime p for every integer a. When p does not divide a, cancelling a yields a^{p−1}≡1. Wilson's theorem characterizes primes by (p−1)!≡−1 mod p. Legendre's formula counts prime factors in factorials: v_p(n!)=Σₖ≥₁⌊n/pᵏ⌋. The valuation of a product is the sum of valuations, and of an integer quotient the difference. A positive valuation means divisibility by p. Before applying Fermat's exponent p−1 form, verify coprimality by factoring the base or ruling out all its prime factors. For factorial quotients, ordinary cancellation is often inefficient; valuation counts handle repeated powers systematically. A counterexample to a universally quantified nondivisibility statement must respect all stated prime restrictions.

similar_questions.prompt: Show 7 divides 10⁶−1.
similar_questions.solution: Since 7 does not divide 10 and 7 is prime, Fermat gives 10⁶≡1 mod 7, proving the divisibility.

similar_questions.prompt: Find v₃(12!).
similar_questions.solution: Legendre gives ⌊12/3⌋+⌊12/9⌋=4+1=5, so 3⁵ divides 12! and 3⁶ does not.

questions.prompt: Let A be a subring of ℚ such that for every nonzero rational r, either r∈A or 1/r∈A. Which statement is FALSE?

options.A: {a∈A:1/a∉A}∪{0} is an additive subgroup of ℚ.
options.B: A has at most one maximal ideal.
options.C: If A≠ℚ, A has infinitely many prime ideals.
options.D: For any nonzero a,b∈A, a divides b or b divides a in A.

hints: The hypothesis makes A a valuation ring: compare a/b and b/a.
Use the localization ℤ_(2), whose denominators are odd, as a counterexample to the prime-ideal claim.
questions.solution: The hypothesis applied to 1 implies 1∈A. For a,b≠0 in A, a/b or b/a lies in A, hence one divides the other, proving D. Let m be zero together with the nonunits. If a,b are nonzero nonunits, suppose b/a∈A (the other case is symmetric); then a+b=a(1+b/a) cannot be a unit, since that would make a a unit. Negation and multiplication by ring elements preserve nonunits, so m is an ideal and in particular an additive subgroup. Every proper ideal contains only nonunits, and A/m is a field; thus m is the unique maximal ideal unless A is already a field (then m={0} is maximal). For C take A=ℤ_(2)={m/n:n odd}. It has the required reciprocal property, is not ℚ, and its only prime ideals are (0) and 2A. Indeed localization retains precisely prime ideals of ℤ disjoint from the odd integers, namely (0),(2). Thus C is false.
questions.theory: A valuation ring of a field K is a subring A in which every nonzero r∈K has r or its reciprocal in A. This condition implies comparability of divisibility for any two nonzero elements of A. The nonunits form an ideal: comparability factors a sum of nonunits by one of them, and a product containing a nonunit cannot become invertible. Since every element outside this ideal is a unit, it is the unique maximal ideal, so valuation rings are local. The localization ℤ_(p) consists of fractions with denominator not divisible by p and is a discrete valuation ring. Its prime ideals are (0) and pℤ_(p), obtained from prime ideals of ℤ avoiding the multiplicative set. A proper subring of a field need not have infinitely many prime ideals; locality and dimension are separate properties.

similar_questions.prompt: Why is ℤ_(3) a valuation ring of ℚ?
similar_questions.solution: Write a rational in lowest terms m/n. If 3∤n it lies in ℤ_(3). If 3|n, coprimality gives 3∤m, so its reciprocal n/m lies there.

similar_questions.prompt: Identify units and maximal ideal of ℤ_(5).
similar_questions.solution: A fraction m/n with 5∤n is invertible precisely when 5∤m. Nonunits have numerator divisible by 5 and form 5ℤ_(5), the unique maximal ideal.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true?

options.A: The ideal 2ℤ[i] is maximal in ℤ[i].
options.B: The ideal Xℂ[X,Y] is maximal in ℂ[X,Y].
options.C: Polynomials in ℂ[X] whose coefficients sum to 0 form a maximal ideal.
options.D: The ideal (√2−1)ℤ[√2] is maximal in ℤ[√2].

hints: An ideal is maximal exactly when the quotient is a field.
Summing coefficients is evaluation at X=1; check whether √2−1 is a unit.
questions.solution: Evaluation ev₁:ℂ[X]→ℂ is onto, and its kernel consists exactly of polynomials whose coefficient sum is zero, namely (X−1). The quotient is ℂ, a field, so C is true. A is false: in ℤ[i]/(2), i+1 is a nonzero nilpotent, since (i+1)²=2i=0, so the quotient is not a field. B has quotient ℂ[Y], not a field. D is the whole ring because (√2−1)(√2+1)=1; a maximal ideal must be proper.
questions.theory: For a commutative ring with identity, a proper ideal I is maximal if and only if R/I is a field, and prime if and only if the quotient is an integral domain. A surjective ring homomorphism to a field therefore has maximal kernel by the first isomorphism theorem. Evaluation at a point a maps K[X] onto the field K and has kernel (X−a), giving a standard maximal ideal. In several variables, removing only one variable usually leaves a polynomial ring, which is not a field. An ideal generated by a unit equals the entire ring and cannot be maximal. Nonzero nilpotents in a quotient disprove that it is a domain or field. Check properness and the actual quotient rather than assuming that a familiar prime integer remains prime in a larger ring.

similar_questions.prompt: Is (X−2) maximal in ℝ[X]?
similar_questions.solution: Evaluation at 2 has kernel (X−2) and image ℝ. Thus ℝ[X]/(X−2)≅ℝ is a field, so the ideal is maximal.

similar_questions.prompt: Is (X,Y) maximal in ℂ[X,Y]?
similar_questions.solution: Evaluation at (0,0) maps onto ℂ and has kernel (X,Y). The quotient is ℂ, hence the ideal is maximal.

questions.prompt: S={1,2,3,4,5} has topology τ={∅,{1},S}. How many homeomorphisms of S onto itself exist?
hints: A homeomorphism must preserve the unique nonempty proper open set.
After fixing 1, the remaining four points may be freely permuted.
questions.solution: For a bijection h:S→S, continuity requires h⁻¹({1}) to be open. This preimage is a singleton, and the only open singleton is {1}, so h(1)=1. Conversely every bijection fixing 1 preserves ∅,{1},S and its inverse does too, hence is a homeomorphism. There are 4!=24 permutations of the other four points.
questions.theory: A topology on a set specifies the open subsets and must contain the empty set and whole space, be closed under arbitrary unions, and under finite intersections. A function is continuous when inverse images of open sets are open. A homeomorphism is a bijection whose map and inverse are continuous; it preserves the full topology, not just the underlying cardinality. On a finite space, identifying distinguished open sets can dramatically restrict allowable permutations. For the topology consisting only of ∅, one singled-out singleton, and the whole set, that unique open singleton must be fixed. All other points have identical topological roles and may be permuted freely. A bijection alone need not be a homeomorphism, and counting all n! permutations ignores any distinguished open subsets.

similar_questions.prompt: On a four-point set with topology {∅,{a},S}, count self-homeomorphisms.
similar_questions.solution: They must fix a; every permutation of the remaining three points works. Thus the count is 3!=6.

similar_questions.prompt: Count self-homeomorphisms of a three-point discrete space.
similar_questions.solution: Every subset is open, so every bijection and its inverse are continuous. All 3!=6 permutations are homeomorphisms.

questions.solution: Set y=xv. Then y′=v+xv′, y″=2v′+xv″, and xy′−y=x²v′. The ODE becomes 2v′+xv″−(2+x)v′=x(v″−v′)=0. Since x>0, v″−v′=0, so v′=Ceˣ and v=a+beˣ. Thus y=x(a+beˣ). questions.theory: A homogeneous linear second-order differential equation y″+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=0 has a two-dimensional solution space on an interval where its coefficients are continuous. If a nonzero solution y₁ is known, reduction of order sets y=y₁v, and the term proportional to v disappears because y₁ already satisfies the equation. The resulting equation involves v′ and v″ and can be reduced to a first-order equation for v′. Dividing by y₁ requires an interval where it does not vanish. Two solutions form a fundamental system if their Wronskian y₁y₂′−y₁′y₂ is nonzero at a point; then every solution is their linear combination. Domain restrictions matter when coefficients have singularities such as 1/x or 1/x². Carefully expand composite expressions such as xy′−y before substituting.

questions.prompt: Let λₙ be the eigenvalues of (xy′)′+(λ/x)y=0 on 1<x<e^{2π}, with y(1)=y(e^{2π})=0. Find Σₙ≥₁1/λₙ.

questions.solution: Since y′=Y′/x, xy′=Y′ and (xy′)′=Y″/x. Multiplication by x gives Y″+λY=0, with Y(0)=Y(2π)=0. λ≤0 yields only the zero solution. For λ>0, Y=C sin(√λt), and sin(2π√λ)=0 implies √λ=n/2, n≥1. Thus λₙ=n²/4. Consequently Σ1/λₙ=4Σ1/n²=4·π²/6=2π²/3.
questions.theory: A Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem seeks values of a parameter λ for which a homogeneous second-order equation has a nonzero solution satisfying both endpoint conditions. The regular form is −(py′)′+qy=λwy, with p and w positive on a finite interval. For the logarithmic coefficients p=x and w=1/x, the substitution t=log x removes these variable coefficients. The basic Dirichlet problem −Y″=λY on an interval of length L has eigenfunctions sin(nπt/L) and eigenvalues (nπ/L)² for n≥1. Zero and negative λ produce no nonzero solutions with both endpoints zero. Reciprocal eigenvalue sums then use the Basel identity Σ1/n²=π²/6. Track the transformed interval length carefully, since it enters eigenvalues quadratically.

similar_questions.prompt: Find Dirichlet eigenvalues of −Y″=λY on (0,π).
similar_questions.solution: Boundary conditions give Y=C sin(√λt) and √λπ=nπ. Hence λₙ=n², and reciprocal sum is π²/6.

similar_questions.prompt: For (xy′)′+(λ/x)y=0 on (1,e³) with zero endpoints, find the reciprocal eigenvalue sum.
similar_questions.solution: t=log x gives interval length 3, so λₙ=(nπ/3)². The sum is (9/π²)(π²/6)=3/2.

questions.solution: The initial condition immediately gives u(1,1)=1+1=2. To check the remaining choices, let u=x+B(y). Substitution gives (y+x+B)+yB′=x−y, hence yB′+B=−2y. Thus (yB)′=−2y and B=C/y−y. Since B(1)=1, C=2. Therefore u=x−y+2/y, which directly satisfies both the PDE and initial data. It gives u(2,2)=1, u(3,3)=2/3, u(4,4)=1/2, so only A holds. The initial line is noncharacteristic because its y-direction characteristic speed is y=1; characteristic uniqueness identifies this smooth solution on y>0.
questions.theory: A first-order quasilinear PDE a(x,y,u)uₓ+b(x,y,u)uᵧ=c(x,y,u) can be solved along characteristics satisfying dx/ds=a, dy/ds=b, du/ds=c. Initial values prescribed on a curve determine a locally unique solution when the characteristic vector is not tangent to that curve, assuming smooth coefficients. Here the initial curve y=1 is noncharacteristic because b=y is nonzero. Before solving a full Cauchy problem, inspect whether a requested value lies directly on the initial curve. An affine ansatz in x can simplify linear dependence in the equation, but it must be verified by substitution and the boundary data. A constructed smooth solution must satisfy both constraints, and uniqueness gives its relevance. Division by y is permitted only on the stated positive-y domain.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve yuᵧ+u=2y with u(x,1)=3, independent of x.

questions.theory: The one-dimensional wave equation u_tt=c²u_xx describes waves travelling at speed c. Sufficient smoothness of f and g ensures that this is a classical solution, and the formula satisfies both initial conditions. The displacement contributes an average of two travelling profiles, while the velocity contributes an integral over the domain of dependence. Polynomial initial data allow an alternative polynomial ansatz and an easy derivative check. Do not omit the integral term when initial velocity is nonzero, and do not confuse its factor 1/(2c) with a simple endpoint average.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve u_tt=u_xx with f(x)=x and g(x)=0.
similar_questions.solution: The formula gives [(x+t)+(x−t)]/2=x. It is independent of time and has zero initial velocity.

similar_questions.prompt: With f(x)=0 and g(x)=2, find u(x,t).
similar_questions.solution: The integral term is (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t}2ds=2t. Thus u=2t, which has u_t(x,0)=2 and both second derivatives zero.

questions.prompt: A cubic spline on [0,4] is s(x)=a(x−2)²+b(x−1)² for 0≤x≤1, (x−2)² for 1<x≤3, and 2c(x−2)²+(x−3)³ for 3<x≤4. Find 2a+b+2c.

Match at x=1 to determine a,b and at x=3 to determine c.
questions.solution: At x=1, continuity gives a=1. First derivatives give −2a=−2, consistent. Matching second derivatives gives 2a+2b=2, hence b=0. At x=3, values give 2c=1, so c=1/2. The first-derivative equality 4c=2 and second-derivative equality 4c=2 agree, since the added cubic has zero value, first derivative, and second derivative at 3. Therefore 2a+b+2c=2+0+1=3.
questions.theory: A cubic spline is a function that is polynomial of degree at most three on each interval between knots and is twice continuously differentiable across the knots. Degree at most three includes quadratic and linear pieces. At every interior knot, the left and right limits of the function, its first derivative, and its second derivative must agree. The third derivative is allowed to jump. Terms of the form (x−k)³ introduced to the right of a knot k automatically vanish together with their first two derivatives at that knot, making them natural spline building blocks. Determine unknown coefficients through matching conditions and then check consistency of all derivative orders. A cubic spline is not necessarily a natural spline; zero endpoint second derivatives require an additional explicit condition.

similar_questions.prompt: Is s(x)=x² for x≤1 and x²+(x−1)³ for x>1 a cubic spline?
similar_questions.solution: At 1 the added term and its first two derivatives are zero. Both pieces have degree at most 3, so s is C² and is a cubic spline.

similar_questions.prompt: For s(x)=ax² on x≤1 and x²+b(x−1)² on x>1, impose C² matching.
similar_questions.solution: Value matching gives a=1. First derivatives then agree. Second derivative matching gives 2a=2+2b, so b=0.

questions.prompt: Let y be an extremal of J[y]=∫₀^{π/4}[(y′)²−4y²+2xy]dx with y(0)=0,y(π/4)=1. Find y(x).
hints: Use the Euler–Lagrange equation d/dx(F_y′)−F_y=0.

questions.solution: For F=(y′)²−4y²+2xy, F_y′=2y′ and F_y=−8y+2x. Thus 2y″+8y−2x=0, or y″+4y=x. General solution: y=Acos2x+Bsin2x+x/4. At 0, y=0 gives A=0. At π/4, sin(π/2)=1 and x/4=π/16, so B=1−π/16. Hence the extremal is (1−π/16)sin2x+x/4.
questions.theory: For a functional J[y]=∫F(x,y,y′)dx with fixed endpoint values, a sufficiently smooth extremal satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation F_y−d(F_y′)/dx=0. It follows from the first variation: vary y by εη with η zero at the endpoints, integrate the derivative term by parts, and use the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations. The Euler–Lagrange equation is a necessary stationarity condition; it does not automatically prove a minimum or maximum. Quadratic functionals commonly lead to linear second-order boundary-value equations. Solve the homogeneous equation, add a particular solution, then impose both endpoint conditions. Carefully differentiate mixed terms such as 2xy with respect to y, treating x as independent. The sign of a y² term determines the sign in the resulting differential equation.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the extremal of ∫₀¹(y′)²dx with y(0)=0,y(1)=2.
similar_questions.solution: Euler–Lagrange gives 2y″=0, so y=A+Bx. Boundary values give A=0,B=2 and y=2x.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the extremal of ∫₀¹[(y′)²+2y]dx with zero endpoints.
similar_questions.solution: Euler–Lagrange yields 2y″−2=0, hence y=x²+Ax+B. The endpoints give B=0,A=−1, so y=x²−x.

questions.solution: Set K=∫₀¹ty(t)dt. Then y(x)=x²+2Kx, and K=∫₀¹(t³+2Kt²)dt=1/4+2K/3. Thus K=3/4 and y=x²+(3/2)x, with y′=2x+3/2. The four left sides are 5/2,2,5,3 respectively, so only D matches. The nonzero coefficient 1−2/3 ensures uniqueness.
questions.theory: A Fredholm integral equation of the second kind has form y(x)=f(x)+λ∫_a^bK(x,t)y(t)dt. A separable or degenerate kernel K(x,t)=Σa_j(x)b_j(t) reduces the unknown integral contribution to finitely many constants c_j=∫b_j(t)y(t)dt. Substituting y=f+λΣa_jc_j into those definitions produces a finite linear system. For a rank-one kernel a(x)b(t), the scalar equation is c=∫bf+λc∫ba. If 1−λ∫ba≠0, a unique solution follows; if it vanishes, compatibility determines whether there are no solutions or infinitely many. Treat the dummy integration variable t separately from the free variable x. Once the explicit solution is obtained, derivatives and endpoint sums can be evaluated directly and checked by substitution. Always check the computed solution in the original equation.

questions.prompt: A dynamical system has L= q̇₁²+q̇₂²+q₁²+q̇₁q̇₂. If p₁,p₂ are the conjugate momenta, which is true?
hints: Conjugate momentum is pᵢ=∂L/∂q̇ᵢ.

questions.solution: The momenta are p₁=2q̇₁+q̇₂ and p₂=2q̇₂+q̇₁. Euler–Lagrange equations give ṗ₁=∂L/∂q₁=2q₁ and ṗ₂=∂L/∂q₂=0, because q₂ does not occur explicitly. Therefore A is correct. The velocity cross term affects the definitions of momenta, but not these explicit coordinate derivatives.
questions.theory: In Lagrangian mechanics, a Lagrangian L(q,q̇,t) determines motion by d(∂L/∂q̇ᵢ)/dt=∂L/∂qᵢ. The conjugate momentum pᵢ is defined as ∂L/∂q̇ᵢ, so its derivative is the coordinate derivative of L along solutions. A coordinate absent from L is called cyclic or ignorable, and its conjugate momentum is conserved even if that momentum contains several velocities. A mixed kinetic term q̇₁q̇₂ couples the momentum definitions. One must use the actual sign of the potential-related term as displayed: if L contains +q₁², its derivative is +2q₁, regardless of the usual convention L=T−V. A nonsingular velocity Hessian permits inversion from momenta to velocities, but that inversion is unnecessary when only momentum derivatives are requested.

similar_questions.prompt: For L=(m/2)q̇²−(k/2)q², find p and ṗ.
similar_questions.solution: p=mq̇ and ṗ=−kq, giving the harmonic-oscillator equation mq̈+kq=0.

similar_questions.prompt: For L=q̇₁²+q̇₂²+3q̇₁q̇₂ with no coordinate dependence, identify conserved momenta.
similar_questions.solution: p₁=2q̇₁+3q̇₂ and p₂=2q̇₂+3q̇₁. Both coordinate derivatives vanish, so ṗ₁=ṗ₂=0.

questions.prompt: A data set has 2n+1 observations (n∈ℕ), each equal to x or x+r, where x∈ℕ,r≥0. Which is always true?

options.A: Mean and median differ if and only if r>0.
options.B: Variance is positive if and only if r>0.
options.C: Mean and mode are equal if and only if r=0.
options.D: Median and mode are equal for every r≥0.

hints: For r>0, the two frequencies sum to an odd number.
One value therefore occurs at least n+1 times and occupies the median position.
questions.solution: If r=0 all observations equal x, so median=mode=x. If r>0, let k be the frequency of x and 2n+1−k that of x+r. Since their sum is odd, the frequencies are unequal and one exceeds n. That majority value is the unique mode and also the (n+1)st ordered observation, hence the median. Thus D always holds. A,B,C are not always true: the wording permits all observations to equal x even when r>0, giving equal mean, median, mode and zero variance. If both distinct values occur, mean is strictly between them, but this extra assumption was not stated.
questions.theory: The arithmetic mean is the sum of observations divided by their number. For an odd sample size 2n+1, the median is the (n+1)st observation after ordering. The mode is the value with greatest frequency; it is unique when one value has a strict frequency majority. In a data set taking at most two distinct values and having odd size, one frequency exceeds half the total, so the median and mode coincide. Variance measures squared deviations from the mean and is zero precisely when all observations are equal, regardless of whether the list of allowed values contains another possible value. The statement that observations are either a or b does not require both to occur. This distinction is essential when testing “if and only if” claims involving a separation parameter.

similar_questions.prompt: For observations 2,2,2,5,5, find mean, median, mode.
similar_questions.solution: Mean=(6+10)/5=16/5=3.2. The third ordered value is 2, and 2 occurs three times, so median=mode=2.

similar_questions.prompt: For seven observations each allowed to be 4 or 9, can variance be zero?
similar_questions.solution: Yes: take all seven equal to 4. Their mean is 4 and every squared deviation is zero, although the two allowed values differ.

questions.solution: There are three primes and three nonprimes, so 3(2p)+3p=9p=1 and p=1/9. Odd faces 1,3,5 have probabilities p,2p,2p. Their sum is 5p=5/9. The number 1 is nonprime.
questions.theory: A discrete probability distribution assigns nonnegative probabilities to possible outcomes, with total probability one. When relative weights are given, normalize by dividing each weight by the sum of all weights. An event probability is the sum of the probabilities of its constituent mutually exclusive outcomes. A prime integer has exactly two positive divisors, one and itself; among the die faces 1 through 6, the primes are 2,3,5, while 1 is not prime. Biased dice need not assign equal probability to each face, so counting favourable faces alone is insufficient. If probabilities are constant within categories and one category has twice the per-face probability of another, category sizes must still be included in the normalization. Separate per-outcome weights from the total probability of a category.

similar_questions.prompt: A four-faced die has weights 1,1,2,2. Find the probability of face 3.
similar_questions.solution: Total weight is 6; face 3 has weight 2, giving probability 2/6=1/3.

similar_questions.prompt: A six-faced die assigns weight 3 to even faces and 1 to odd faces. Find P(result>4).

questions.prompt: Z₁,Z₂,… are iid discrete uniform on {1,2,…,2024}. Put Yₙ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿZᵢ for n≥2 and let Xₙ be the remainder of Yₙ modulo 2025. Which is true?
hints: From any residue, the next increment reaches every other residue with equal probability.
Let pₙ=P(Xₙ=0); derive pₙ₊₁=(1−pₙ)/2024.
questions.solution: A nonzero increment modulo 2025 cannot leave a residue unchanged. From each nonzero current residue, exactly one of the 2024 increments takes it to zero. Hence pₙ₊₁=(1−pₙ)/2024. Its fixed point p satisfies 2024p=1−p, giving p=1/2025. Moreover pₙ₊₁−1/2025=−(pₙ−1/2025)/2024, so the deviations decay geometrically and the limit is 1/2025.
questions.theory: A random walk modulo an integer m is a finite-state Markov chain whose transition probabilities depend only on the current residue and the increment law. If the increment is uniform on all nonzero residues, a transition is equally likely to any different state and impossible to the same state. The uniform distribution on the m states is stationary because each transition-matrix column sums to one. For a specific target state, its probability satisfies pₙ₊₁=(1−pₙ)/(m−1), with fixed point 1/m. Subtracting the fixed point produces a geometric recurrence with multiplier −1/(m−1), whose magnitude is below one for m>2. This directly proves convergence without a general Markov-chain theorem. Distinguish the number m of possible remainders from the m−1 possible nonzero increments.

similar_questions.prompt: Uniformly add 1,2,3,4 modulo 5. Find the limiting probability of residue 0.
similar_questions.solution: The recursion is pₙ₊₁=(1−pₙ)/4, so its fixed point is 1/5 and deviations have factor −1/4. The limit is 1/5.

similar_questions.prompt: Uniformly add 1 modulo 2 starting at residue 0. Does the zero-state probability converge?
similar_questions.solution: The state alternates deterministically between 0 and 1. Thus pₙ alternates 1 and 0; the recurrence multiplier is −1, so convergence fails.

questions.prompt: Brand I battery life has density e^{−x} for x>0. Brand II has density (x/4)e^{−x/2} for x>0. Mobiles use I and II with probabilities 20% and 80%. Find the probability battery life exceeds 2 years.
hints: Use total probability over the two battery brands.
Integrate the Brand II density from 2 to infinity; integration by parts gives 2e^{−1}.
questions.solution: For Brand I, survival probability is ∫₂∞e^{−x}dx=e^{−2}. For Brand II, an antiderivative of (x/4)e^{−x/2} is −(x/2+1)e^{−x/2}; its tail at 2 equals 2e^{−1}. Thus P(T>2)=(1/5)e^{−2}+(4/5)(2e^{−1})=(1/5)(e^{−2}+8e^{−1}).
questions.theory: The survival function of a nonnegative continuous random variable is S(t)=P(T>t)=∫_t^∞f(x)dx. An exponential distribution with rate λ has survival e^{−λt}; a gamma distribution with shape two and scale β has density xe^{−x/β}/β² and survival e^{−t/β}(1+t/β), obtainable by integration by parts. When a population is a mixture of brands or subgroups, the law of total probability weights each conditional survival probability by its subgroup proportion. The mixture distribution is generally not itself an exponential or gamma distribution with averaged parameters. Rates and scales are reciprocals, so identify the density carefully before using a formula. Population proportions apply to the conditional probabilities, not to the time threshold or to the density parameters.

similar_questions.prompt: Half a population has Exp(1) life and half Exp(2). Find survival at t=1.
similar_questions.solution: Total probability gives (1/2)e^{−1}+(1/2)e^{−2}; averaging the rates would not give this same mixture.

questions.prompt: X has P(X=0)=θ/3, P(X=1)=1−θ/2, P(X=2)=θ/6, θ∈(0,1). A sample of size 90 has counts 20,60,10 for 0,1,2. Find the maximum likelihood estimate of θ.
hints: Ignoring constants, the likelihood is θ³⁰(1−θ/2)⁶⁰.
Differentiate its logarithm and solve the score equation.
questions.solution: The likelihood is proportional to (θ/3)²⁰(1−θ/2)⁶⁰(θ/6)¹⁰, hence θ³⁰(1−θ/2)⁶⁰. Its log derivative is 30/θ−30/(1−θ/2). Setting this to zero gives θ=1−θ/2 and θ=2/3. The second derivative −30/θ²−15/(1−θ/2)² is strictly negative, so this interior point is the unique maximum. It lies in (0,1).
questions.theory: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameter values maximizing the probability or density of the observed sample. For iid discrete observations recorded as category counts n_j, the likelihood is proportional to ∏p_j(θ)^{n_j}; the multinomial coefficient is constant in θ and can be dropped. Taking logarithms turns products into sums and preserves maximizers because the logarithm is increasing. An interior candidate solves the score equation, the derivative of the log likelihood. Strict negative second derivative establishes uniqueness of a maximum on an interval, but one must also check the parameter restrictions and possible boundary behavior. Categories sharing the same parameter factor can be combined in the score. Keep the chain-rule factor when differentiating log(1−θ/2), and distinguish likelihood maximization from simply equating every observed frequency with its model probability.

similar_questions.prompt: A Bernoulli sample has 12 successes and 8 failures. Find the MLE of p.
similar_questions.solution: Log likelihood is 12log p+8log(1−p). The score gives 12/p=8/(1−p), so p=12/20=.6; strict concavity confirms the maximum.

similar_questions.prompt: P(0)=θ/4,P(1)=1−θ/2,P(2)=θ/4, with counts 10,30,10. Find the interior MLE.
similar_questions.solution: Likelihood is proportional to θ²⁰(1−θ/2)³⁰. Score 20/θ−15/(1−θ/2)=0 gives 20−10θ=15θ, so θ=.8.

questions.prompt: One observation X has density f(x|θ)=3(θ−x)²/θ³ for 0<x<θ, zero otherwise. The interval (X/(1−λ₁),X/(1−λ₂)) has confidence coefficient 1−α, with 0<λ₁<λ₂<1. Which holds?
hints: The pivot W=1−X/θ has a parameter-free density.
Translate interval coverage into λ₁<W<λ₂.
questions.solution: Set V=X/θ; its density is 3(1−v)² for 0<v<1. Thus W=1−V has density 3w² on (0,1). The event X/(1−λ₁)<θ<X/(1−λ₂) is equivalent to 1−λ₂<X/θ<1−λ₁, hence λ₁<W<λ₂. Its probability is ∫_{λ₁}^{λ₂}3w²dw=λ₂³−λ₁³. Equating coverage to 1−α proves B.
questions.theory: A confidence interval is a random interval whose probability of covering the fixed unknown parameter equals a stated confidence coefficient under repeated sampling. A pivotal quantity is a function of the data and parameter with a distribution independent of the parameter; scale families often use X/θ. A one-to-one transformation of a continuous random variable changes its density by the absolute Jacobian of the inverse. Once a pivot's distribution is known, translate the coverage inequalities into bounds for that pivot and integrate its density. Care is needed when reciprocals or subtraction reverse inequalities. Strict versus non-strict endpoints do not affect coverage for continuous distributions. The coverage probability concerns the random data, whereas θ stays fixed; it is not a posterior probability assigned to θ.

similar_questions.prompt: If X is uniform on (0,θ), find coverage of (X/b,X/a), 0<a<b<1.
similar_questions.solution: The event is a<X/θ<b. Since X/θ is uniform on (0,1), coverage is b−a.

similar_questions.prompt: If W has density 2w on (0,1), find P(a<W<b).
similar_questions.solution: Integrating gives ∫_a^b2w dw=b²−a². Thus that interval has target coverage 1−α when b²−a²=1−α.

questions.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid with density θ2^θ/x^{θ+1} for x>2, θ>0. Define χ²_{m,β} by P(Y>χ²_{m,β})=β for Y~χ²_m. For testing H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ>1, which is the size-α UMP rejection rule?
hints: Tᵢ=log(Xᵢ/2) has an exponential distribution with rate θ.
Large θ gives smaller sums, and under the null 2ΣTᵢ has χ²_{2n} distribution.
questions.solution: The survival P(X>2eᵗ)=e^{−θt} shows Tᵢ=log(Xᵢ/2)~Exp(rate θ). Their sum T=Σlog Xᵢ−nlog2 has likelihood θⁿe^{−θT}. For any θ>1 the likelihood ratio to θ=1 is θⁿe^{−(θ−1)T}, decreasing in T; the same lower-tail rejection set is most powerful for every alternative. Under H₀, 2T~χ²_{2n}. With the specified upper-tail quantile notation, P(2T<χ²_{2n,1−α})=α. Hence reject when Σlog Xᵢ<(1/2)χ²_{2n,1−α}+nlog2, option B.
questions.theory: A uniformly most powerful test maximizes power among all tests of a given size for every parameter in the specified alternative. The Neyman–Pearson lemma chooses large likelihood ratios for a simple alternative, and monotone likelihood ratios in a common statistic can yield the same rejection region across a one-sided family. Pareto-type scale observations become exponential variables under logarithmic transformation: log(X/a) has rate θ. A sum of n iid rate-one exponentials is gamma with shape n and scale one, and twice that sum is chi-square with 2n degrees of freedom. Increasing the exponential rate shifts observations downward, so the relevant rejection tail is lower. Quantile conventions must be read carefully: an upper-tail probability 1−α corresponds to a lower-tail probability α.

similar_questions.prompt: Test Exp(rate θ) observations for θ=1 versus θ>1. State a size .05 rejection region for n observations.
similar_questions.solution: Let T be their sum. Under the null 2T~χ²_{2n}; reject for 2T below the lower .05 quantile, equivalently below the upper-tail .95 quantile.

similar_questions.prompt: For one Exp(1) observation, find the lower-tail .1 cutoff.
similar_questions.solution: P(T<c)=1−e^{−c}=.1 gives c=−log(.9). A test against a larger rate rejects when T<−log(.9).

questions.prompt: X|θ~N(θ,15), and the improper prior on θ is proportional to 1 on ℝ. Observed X=13. Which statement is true?

options.A: Posterior mean=MLE of θ; posterior variance=Var(X|θ).
options.B: Posterior mean=MLE of θ; posterior variance<Var(X|θ).
options.C: Posterior mean>MLE of θ; posterior variance=Var(X|θ).
options.D: Posterior mean>MLE of θ; posterior variance<Var(X|θ).

hints: The flat prior leaves the likelihood kernel unchanged as a function of θ.
Normalize exp[−(θ−13)²/(2·15)] as a normal density in θ.
questions.solution: The likelihood as a function of θ is proportional to exp[−(13−θ)²/30]. Multiplication by the constant prior gives this same kernel, whose normalized posterior is N(13,15). Thus posterior mean is 13 and posterior variance is 15. The likelihood is maximized at θ=13, so the posterior mean equals the MLE, and posterior variance equals the conditional observation variance. A is correct.
questions.theory: Bayes' formula gives a posterior density proportional to likelihood times prior, provided the product has a finite positive normalizing integral. A constant prior on the whole real line is improper because it does not integrate to one, but it can yield a proper posterior. For a normal observation with known variance σ² and unknown mean θ, the likelihood in θ is a normal kernel centered at the observed value. A flat prior therefore produces N(x,σ²). With n independent observations it instead produces N(x̄,σ²/n). A proper normal prior adds precision and generally shrinks both the posterior mean and variance. Do not assume every Bayesian update reduces variance relative to the sampling variance; with one observation and a flat prior they are equal.

similar_questions.prompt: Two iid N(θ,8) observations are 3 and 5, with flat prior. Find posterior.
similar_questions.solution: The sample mean is 4. Completing the likelihood square gives posterior N(4,8/2)=N(4,4).

similar_questions.prompt: X|θ~N(θ,4) and θ~N(0,4); observe X=6. Find posterior.
similar_questions.solution: Precisions add: posterior variance=(1/4+1/4)⁻¹=2. Mean=2(6/4+0/4)=3, so posterior is N(3,2).

questions.prompt: For yᵢ=β₀+β₁x₁ᵢ+⋯+β₈x₈ᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,…,29, with iid N(0,σ²) errors, the least-squares F statistic for regression significance is 2.50. Find possible R² and adjusted R².
hints: There are p=8 slope terms and n−p−1=20 residual degrees of freedom.
questions.solution: F=(SSR/8)/(SSE/20)=(20/8)R²/(1−R²). Since F=2.5=20/8, R²/(1−R²)=1, giving R²=.5. Adjusted R²=1−(SSE/20)/(SST/28)=1−(1−.5)(28/20)=1−.7=.3. Thus option B is correct.
questions.theory: In ordinary least-squares regression with an intercept, total corrected sum of squares decomposes as SST=SSR+SSE. The coefficient of determination is R²=SSR/SST=1−SSE/SST. For n observations and p slope predictors, the global F statistic testing all slopes equal zero is (SSR/p)/(SSE/(n−p−1)), assuming a full-rank design matrix. Under independent normal errors with common variance, it has an F distribution under the null. Adjusted R² accounts for degrees of freedom: 1−[SSE/(n−p−1)]/[SST/(n−1)]. It can be negative and is generally lower than ordinary R². The intercept consumes one degree of freedom but is not counted among the p slopes in the global numerator. Use the same degrees of freedom consistently in both formulas.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=21,p=4,R²=.4, compute F and adjusted R².
similar_questions.solution: Residual degrees of freedom are 16. F=(.4/4)/(.6/16)=8/3. Adjusted R²=1−.6·20/16=.25.

questions.prompt: (X₁,X₂,X₃)ᵀ~N₃(0,I₃), and (X,Y,Z)ᵀ=[[3,0,0],[2,2,0],[4,0,4]](X₁,X₂,X₃)ᵀ. Find the partial correlation ρ_{YZ·X}.
hints: Regress Y and Z on X=3X₁.
Their residuals involve independent coordinates X₂ and X₃.
questions.solution: X=3X₁, Y=2X₁+2X₂ and Z=4X₁+4X₃. The linear projection of Y onto X is (2/3)X and of Z onto X is (4/3)X. The residuals are 2X₂ and 4X₃, independent with positive variances. Their correlation is zero, so ρ_{YZ·X}=0. Equivalently covariance(Y,Z)=8 and covariance(Y,X)covariance(Z,X)/variance(X)=6·12/9=8, leaving zero partial covariance.
questions.theory: Partial correlation between Y and Z controlling for X is the correlation of their residuals after linear projection on X. For nondegenerate variables it equals (ρ_YZ−ρ_YXρ_ZX)/√[(1−ρ_YX²)(1−ρ_ZX²)]. The unstandardized residual covariance is Cov(Y,Z)−Cov(Y,X)Cov(Z,X)/Var(X). In a jointly normal model, zero partial correlation is equivalent to conditional independence given X, provided residual variances are positive. Independent standard normal coordinates make linear transformations easy to analyze: covariances are sums of products of matching coefficients. A common component can create marginal correlation that vanishes after controlling for the variable measuring that component. Determine residuals before normalizing; their independence or zero covariance may make a lengthy correlation calculation unnecessary.

similar_questions.prompt: Let Y=A+B,Z=A+C,X=A with independent unit-variance A,B,C. Find partial correlation.
similar_questions.solution: After projection on X the residuals are B,C. They have covariance zero and variances one, so partial correlation is zero, although marginal correlation is 1/2.

similar_questions.prompt: Let Y=A+B,Z=A+B+C,X=A with independent unit-variance components. Find partial correlation.
similar_questions.solution: Residuals are B and B+C. Their covariance is 1 and variances are 1 and 2, giving ρ=1/√2.

questions.prompt: A population of size 85 contains 34 Statisticians and 51 Biologists. Independent SRSWOR samples draw 12 and 15 from those strata. Let ȳ_S,ȳ_B,ȳ denote the two stratum sample means and pooled sample mean. Which is an unbiased estimator of population mean Ȳ?
hints: Each stratum sample mean is unbiased for its own population mean.
Combine them using population stratum proportions, not sample proportions.
questions.solution: Under SRSWOR, E(ȳ_S)=Ȳ_S and E(ȳ_B)=Ȳ_B. The target mean is (34/85)Ȳ_S+(51/85)Ȳ_B=(2/5)Ȳ_S+(3/5)Ȳ_B. Therefore (2ȳ_S+3ȳ_B)/5 is unbiased. The pooled sample uses weights 12/27=4/9 and 15/27=5/9, not the population weights; option C is precisely that pooled mean. Option D weights the strata 5/9 and 4/9, also incorrect in general.
questions.theory: Stratified sampling divides a finite population into disjoint strata and samples separately within each. Under simple random sampling without replacement, every subset of the required size in a stratum is equally likely and the stratum sample mean is unbiased for its population mean. The overall population mean is the weighted sum of stratum population means with weights W_h=N_h/N. Its unbiased estimator is therefore ΣW_hȳ_h, regardless of how sample sizes are allocated. A pooled unweighted sample mean instead uses n_h/n and is unbiased for the overall mean only under proportional allocation or special equal-mean populations. Without-replacement sampling affects the estimator's variance through finite-population corrections, but not these expectations. Distinguish population sizes from sample sizes when selecting weights; inverse sample-size weights do not generally estimate the desired mean.

similar_questions.prompt: Two strata have population sizes 20,80 and sample means 10,30. Find the stratified estimate.
similar_questions.solution: Weights are .2 and .8, so the estimate is .2·10+.8·30=26, irrespective of sample allocation.

similar_questions.prompt: Strata sizes are 60,40 and sample sizes 6,4. Is the pooled mean unbiased?
similar_questions.solution: The sample proportions .6,.4 equal population proportions, so the pooled mean .6ȳ₁+.4ȳ₂ is the stratified unbiased estimator.

questions.prompt: Maximize z=x+y subject to 5x+3y≤30, 2x+6y≤25, 2x−y≤8, x≥0,y≥0. Find the optimal objective value.
hints: Intersect the first two binding constraints and test the remaining constraint.
A nonnegative weighted sum of the first two inequalities gives a matching objective upper bound.
questions.solution: Solving 5x+3y=30 and 2x+6y=25 gives x=35/8,y=65/24. Both are positive and 2x−y=145/24≤8, so the point is feasible. Its objective is 35/8+65/24=170/24=85/12. To certify optimality, multiply the first inequality by 1/6 and the second by 1/12. The left side becomes x+y and the right side becomes 30/6+25/12=85/12. Every feasible point has z≤85/12, and the constructed point attains this bound.
questions.theory: A linear program optimizes a linear objective over a polyhedron defined by linear inequalities. In two variables the feasible region is an intersection of half-planes, and a finite optimum is attained at a boundary vertex or along an optimal edge when the feasible set is nonempty and bounded in the objective direction. A candidate obtained by intersecting two constraint boundaries must satisfy all remaining inequalities, including nonnegativity. Optimality can be certified without listing every vertex: a nonnegative linear combination of constraint inequalities that equals the objective provides an upper bound for maximization. A feasible point attaining that bound is optimal by weak duality. The multipliers are dual variables, and unused constraints may have multiplier zero. Never accept an intersection solely because it yields a large objective; feasibility is an independent requirement.

similar_questions.prompt: Maximize x+y subject to x+2y≤6,2x+y≤6,x,y≥0.
similar_questions.solution: Adding the two inequalities gives 3(x+y)≤12, hence z≤4. The feasible intersection x=y=2 attains 4, certifying optimality.

similar_questions.prompt: Maximize 2x+y subject to x+y≤3,x≤2,x,y≥0.
similar_questions.solution: Add x+y≤3 to x≤2 to obtain 2x+y≤5. The feasible point (2,1) attains 5, so the maximum is 5.
